## Key caveats

- This is a preliminary, rapid assessment. The product flags abrupt surface change consistent with damage; it is an indicator of likely damage, not a building-by-building census, and it does not confirm damage at any individual building. Individual building-level damage severity cannot be determined from these data alone — detected damage can span from light/moderate (EMS-98 grades 1, 2, and 3) to full collapse.
- Against undamaged controls in low-shaking areas, the false-alarm rate falls from about 3% at the possible tier to about 1% at probable to under 1% at high confidence. This is a floor measured in low-shaking areas; the false-alarm rate inside the strongly-shaken operating zone is not measured, because no reference dataset grades undamaged buildings there.
- Use the analyzed-area layer to distinguish "assessed and not flagged" from "not assessed": unassessed ground should not be mistaken for undamaged.
- Agreement figures against Copernicus EMS, Microsoft AI for Good, and crowd-sourced reports are external cross-checks against datasets with their own coverage limits and errors, not quality-assured ground truth.

# Methodology — Sentinel-1 Coherent Change Detection Building Damage Assessment (EMSR884, Delivery v1)

## How this was made

We map damage with Sentinel-1 radar coherent change detection following methods we have developed in other settings (Scher & Van Den Hoek, 2025, *Science of Remote Sensing*; Scher & Van Den Hoek, 2025, arXiv:2506.14730; full references below). Radar coherence measures how similar a surface's radar echoes are between two satellite overpasses. A sudden loss of coherence between a post-earthquake image and a stack of pre-earthquake references is the decorrelation signal that can indicate damage. We categorize damage in areas that were stable for approximately one year before the earthquake and flag surfaces that changed abruptly after the earthquake, showing a sudden and sharp drop in radar signal correlation between each set of acquisitions collected before and after the tremors.

## Sentinel-1 scenes analyzed

Eight post-earthquake acquisitions (24 June 2026, 22:49 UTC, to 1 July 2026, 10:16 UTC) were each compared against a per-scene, matched-baseline stack of pre-earthquake reference coherence images (260 reference images in total, from 24 April 2025 to 23 June 2026) and merged into a single damage map:

| Sentinel-1 granule | Pre-earthquake coherence images | Post-earthquake coherence images |
|---|---|---|
| S1C_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260624T224958_20260624T225025_008254_010515_304A | 35 | 35 |
| S1D_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260625T101600_20260625T101627_003391_005F73_3489 | 20 | 20 |
| S1A_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260625T223428_20260625T223458_065132_0835CC_E889 | 33 | 33 |
| S1D_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260625T224209_20260625T224239_003399_005FB5_8B0A | 40 | 40 |
| S1C_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260626T223339_20260626T223402_008283_01061B_1BF7 | 33 | 33 |
| S1D_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260630T102431_20260630T102458_003464_0061E9_EA58 | 35 | 35 |
| S1D_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260630T225009_20260630T225040_003472_006226_2543 | 35 | 35 |
| S1C_IW_SLC__1SDV_20260701T101557_20260701T101628_008348_01084F_7E63 | 29 | 29 |

## From pixels to building footprints

We aggregate pixel-based surface disturbance to Overture Maps Foundation building footprint outlines. For each building footprint, we compute a z-score: the deviation of its post-earthquake coherence from roughly one year of pre-earthquake coherence values, measured in standard deviations of that pre-earthquake period. A larger z-score indicates a more anomalous drop in coherence following the earthquake. A building's `damage_confidence` is the highest z-floor it clears over at least half of its footprint area. Each confidence floor corresponds to a one-sided percentile of the pre-earthquake distribution:

| Tier | z-score | Percentile | In binary `damage` layer? |
|---|---|---|---|
| possible | ≥ 1.5 | 93.3rd | no |
| probable | ≥ 2.0 | 97.7th (2 sigma) | yes |
| high_confidence | ≥ 3.0 | 99.87th (3 sigma) | yes |

Across the full assessed area: high_confidence 25,920 buildings; probable 43,511; the binary damage layer (probable + high_confidence union) 69,431; possible (flagged, below the damage threshold) 54,202; all flagged tiers 123,633.

## Agreement and sensitivity analyses

### Crowd-sourced damage reports (Sismo Ayuda VE)

We compared this product against crowd-sourced damage reports from Sismo Ayuda VE, a platform on which Venezuelan engineers record EMS-98 damage grades for individual buildings. These reference data are of unknown quality assurance and may contain errors themselves. We accessed the public endpoint (https://www.sismoayudave.com/api/mapa) on 2026-07-07 at 19:53:33 UTC and retrieved EMS-98 damage grades for 1,427 buildings in the analyzed area (of 1,705 reports). EMS-98 is a damage scale, so every graded building carries some level of damage, from G1 (negligible to slight) through G5 (destruction); these reports contain no undamaged buildings. We therefore assess two things separately: how much reported damage the map detects, by grade, and how often it flags a building that is not damaged, measured against a separate control population.

Graded buildings in the analyzed area: G1 344, G2 535, G3 352, G4 159, G5 37.

**Detection by damage grade.** Detection is the fraction of reported buildings our method flags. A damage report is detected at a given tier if a building at that tier or higher lies within 30 m of the report location — 30 m is the pixel size of our coherence grid, so this is a resolution-consistent tolerance, and the same matching is used in the Copernicus EMS comparison below. Detection was computed on the 1,277 of the 1,427 graded reports (89.5%) that have a mapped building within 30 m. Detection frequency rises with damage severity at every tier:

| EMS-98 grade | Buildings | ≥ possible | ≥ probable | ≥ high confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 (negligible to slight) | 312 | 0.33 | 0.17 | 0.06 |
| G2 (moderate) | 480 | 0.38 | 0.25 | 0.09 |
| G3 (heavy) | 315 | 0.46 | 0.32 | 0.16 |
| G4 (very heavy) | 136 | 0.57 | 0.43 | 0.25 |
| G5 (destruction) | 34 | 0.77 | 0.65 | 0.38 |

Cumulative detection at each severity threshold:

| EMS-98 | Buildings | ≥ possible | ≥ probable | ≥ high confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ≥ G1 (any reported damage) | 1,277 | 0.42 | 0.28 | 0.13 |
| ≥ G2 | 965 | 0.45 | 0.31 | 0.15 |
| ≥ G3 | 485 | 0.51 | 0.38 | 0.20 |
| ≥ G4 | 170 | 0.61 | 0.48 | 0.28 |
| ≥ G5 (destruction) | 34 | 0.77 | 0.65 | 0.38 |

At the probable confidence tier, the map flags 0.28 of all reported-damaged buildings, about one in four, and detection rises with severity from 0.17 at G1 to 0.65 at G5. The product detects collapse and severe structural damage and is weaker on slight and moderate damage.

**False-alarm rate.** Because the Sismo reports contain no undamaged buildings, we measured the false-alarm rate against a separate control population: buildings in low-shaking-intensity zones (USGS ShakeMap MMI ≤ V), matched one-to-one to the reported-damaged buildings on pre-earthquake coherence and building footprint size, so the two groups differ only in whether they were shaken. Applying the same 30 m rule, the false-alarm rate is about 0.011 at the probable confidence tier and about 0.026 at the possible tier. Matching the controls on pre-earthquake coherence alone, without footprint size, keeps the rate low (about 0.024 at the probable tier). This figure is a floor measured in low-shaking areas: the false-alarm rate inside the strongly-shaken operating zone is not measured, because no reference dataset grades undamaged buildings there.

**Consistency with modeled shaking intensity.** As an additional physical-consistency check, independent of any damage reference dataset, we compared the per-building coherence-change z-score against USGS ShakeMap modeled shaking intensity across the full monitored population of approximately 2.7 million buildings. The median per-building z-score rises monotonically with modeled shaking: essentially no change at MMI ≤ V and VI (medians -0.20 and -0.23), a modest shift at MMI VII (+0.10), and a clear coherence loss at MMI VIII (+0.84), where the bulk of the distribution separates from the low-shaking bands. This is a consistency statement rather than damage validation — the z-score measures surface change and MMI is a model estimate — but the independent radar signal strengthens exactly where the shaking model predicts stronger shaking. The near-epicentral San Felipe zone (MMI IX, 3,541 buildings) is omitted from this check because the weak pre-earthquake radar stack there limits coherence sensitivity.

### Copernicus EMS (EMSR884)

Copernicus EMS analysts graded 3,072 buildings by hand (as of our access on 2026-07-03; grading is ongoing) from very high-resolution imagery. Our map detects the overwhelming majority of them, and detects the most severe damage most reliably:

| Damage grade (EMS) | Buildings graded | Detected by us |
|---|---|---|
| Destroyed | 695 | 95% |
| Damaged | 828 | 89% |
| Possibly damaged | 1,549 | 81% |
| All grades | 3,072 | 86% |

Including our lower-confidence "possible" buildings raises the overall figure to 89% of Copernicus EMS detections. At Ciudad Chávez, a reported-collapse site, all 177 graded buildings are detected and we detect additional damaged buildings that Copernicus EMS omits. Detection is strongest along the hard-hit central coast and weaker as distance from the rupture increases.

Where each EMS grade falls among our confidence tiers — the most severely damaged buildings land overwhelmingly in our highest tier, and the share we miss grows as the interpreted damage level decreases in severity:

| Damage grade (EMS) | high confidence | probable | possible | not flagged |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Destroyed | 78% | 17% | 2% | 3% |
| Damaged | 74% | 15% | 2% | 9% |
| Possibly damaged | 66% | 15% | 3% | 16% |

Copernicus EMS grading is expert rapid-mapping, not quality-assured ground truth, but where grading exists it is likely a reliable measure of real damage. Its main limitations are its relatively small spatial coverage and the difficulty of detecting damage that is not readily visible at building rooftops.

### Microsoft AI for Good

Microsoft's AI for Good building-damage layer is model-derived, also not quality-assured ground truth. As a recall check, we detect the highest percentage of Microsoft's damage labels for larger buildings and a smaller share for the smallest footprints (coastal overlap only):

| Building size | Buildings | We detect of Microsoft's damage |
|---|---|---|
| under 50 m² | 27,994 | 49% |
| 50–100 m² | 18,951 | 49% |
| 100–200 m² | 11,207 | 54% |
| 200–500 m² | 4,065 | 67% |
| over 500 m² | 1,241 | 74% |

### Damage we detect beyond the other datasets

A large share of the buildings we flag are not in the Copernicus EMS or Microsoft datasets, for two reasons. First, coverage: there is no EMS grading for much of the greater-Caracas metro (including Petare and Antímano), and Microsoft's assessment was limited to a portion of the coastal strip. Buildings we flag there are simply outside the other datasets' extent, not in disagreement with them. Second, within the area all three cover, we still flag additional buildings that neither reference marks as damaged. These are not scattered noise: they show as strong a coherence drop as the buildings all three sources mark as damaged. A likely reason is that radar responds directly to physical change in a structure (movement, deformation, debris scatter), while in overhead optical imagery a partial collapse can be hard to see — a roof can look intact from above even when the structure beneath has failed. These mechanisms help explain why imaging radar and coherent change detection capture earthquake damage more accurately and comprehensively than satellite optical imagery (Ainscoe et al., 2025, *Communications Earth & Environment*).

As a single-building qualitative check, one high_confidence detection in Catia La Mar was compared against a geolocated ground photograph collected by HOT ChatMap volunteers. This ChatMap comparison is a qualitative visual comparison only (a single illustrative building); no quantitative agreement analysis was performed against the ChatMap data.

## Limitations

- This is a preliminary, rapid assessment. These data reflect abrupt surface change consistent with damage. Individual building-level damage severity cannot be determined from these data alone; detected damage can span from light/moderate (EMS-98 grades 1, 2, and 3) to full collapse. These maps are an indicator of damage, not a building-by-building census, and are not validated against field data with a properly characterized non-damage population of buildings within strong-shaking areas.
- Detection accuracy is computed on the 1,277 of 1,427 graded reports (89.5%) that have a mapped building within 30 m. The 150 reports (10.5%) with no building within 30 m are excluded, and if those are disproportionately small or isolated structures the reported detection is mildly optimistic.
- The false-alarm rate of about 0.011 is a floor measured in low-shaking areas. The false-alarm rate inside the strongly-shaken operating zone is not measured, because no reference grades undamaged buildings there.
- The Copernicus EMS and Microsoft figures are external cross-checks against unvalidated datasets with their own coverage limits and errors.
- The crowd-sourced validation exercise is not based on a quality-controlled EMS-98 grading from a single group of engineers, although the crowd-sourcing project does require engineers to be registered with Venezuela to participate. It has unknown quality assurance as of writing.
- The HOT ChatMap comparison is a qualitative visual comparison only (a single illustrative building); no quantitative agreement analysis was performed against the ChatMap data.

## Data sources and references

- **Copernicus EMS rapid mapping (EMSR884):** https://mapping.emergency.copernicus.eu/activations/EMSR884
- **Microsoft AI for Good — Venezuela 2026 earthquake building damage assessment:** https://visualizers.aiforgood.ai/damage-assessment/venezuela_earthquake_2026_report.html (CC BY 4.0; also distributed via the Humanitarian Data Exchange, HDX).
- **Sismo Ayuda VE** crowdsourced damage reports: https://www.sismoayudave.com/api/mapa (snapshot 2026-07-07 19:53:33 UTC; EMS-98 macroseismic grades; volunteer-assigned).
- **HOT ChatMap damage validation (Venezuela EQ):** building damage grades and geolocated ground photographs collected by HOT ChatMap volunteers (contributions hashtag #2026_LACH_VE_EQ): https://umap.hotosm.org/en/map/damage-validation-buildings-venezuela-eq_3261 (accessed 2026-07-10; the dataset is being published on the Humanitarian Data Exchange, HDX).
- **USGS ShakeMap** (event us6000t7zp): Modified Mercalli Intensity used to define the low-shaking control population.
- Scher, C., & Van Den Hoek, J. (2025). Nationwide conflict damage mapping with interferometric synthetic aperture radar: A study of the 2022 Russia–Ukraine conflict. *Science of Remote Sensing*, 11, 100217. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.srs.2025.100217
- Scher, C., & Van Den Hoek, J. (2025). Active InSAR monitoring of building damage in Gaza during the Israel–Hamas War. *arXiv preprint* arXiv:2506.14730. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14730
- Ainscoe, E. A., Swaminathan, R., Way, L., Modugno, S., Chin, S. T., Panta, N., Crevoisier, T., & Yun, S.-H. (2025). Earthquake damage mapped more comprehensively and accurately by radar satellites than optical imagery. *Communications Earth & Environment*, 6, 631. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02623-4

notes:
# Venezuela Earthquake — Sentinel-1 Radar Building Damage Assessment (Delivery v1)

A rapid assessment of building damage from the 24 June 2026 Venezuela earthquake (M7.5 mainshock, M7.2 foreshock), centered near San Felipe and Yumare in north-central Venezuela, with strong shaking along the central coast and into greater Caracas.

A preliminary version (v0) of this product was released on 27 June 2026 via the NASA Disaster Response and Coordination System. This second iteration (v1) expands area coverage: post-event Sentinel-1 acquisitions that were not available at the first release (v0) filled the coverage gaps within the Copernicus EMS / USGS ShakeMap Modified Mercalli Intensity ≥ VI (strong-shaking) area, raising coverage of that hazard-provenanced, damage-onset zone to 100% and increasing the number of Overture building footprints under monitoring by 26.5% (from 2,133,587 to 2,699,969, an increase of 566,382 footprints). We extended the Copernicus EMSR884 area of interest to a latitude of approximately 11.04°N to include all areas with strong shaking.

Using Sentinel-1 satellite radar coherent change detection, we estimate **69,431 buildings were likely damaged or destroyed**, as of the most recent analyzed satellite pass on 1 July 2026 (10:16 UTC). The assessment covers the entire area activated under Copernicus EMS activation EMSR884 (USGS event us6000t7zp) and is a preliminary product. These data reflect abrupt surface change consistent with damage — a damage indicator, not a confirmation of damage for any individual building.

Each building footprint carries a confidence tier (**possible / probable / high_confidence**) instead of the numeric damage probability score used in the previous delivery. The confidence tier **does not represent individual building-level damage severity**. Instead, it represents how anomalous the post-earthquake interferometric coherence was compared to roughly one year prior to the earthquake. This is described in more detail in the README and slide deck PDFs included below.

## Coverage and dates

- **Post-event:** Sentinel-1 swaths from 24 June 2026 (22:49 UTC) to 1 July 2026 (10:16 UTC), spanning eight post-earthquake acquisitions.
- **Pre-event:** 260 reference coherence images — per-scene matched-baseline stacks — from 24 April 2025 to 23 June 2026.
- **Monitored universe:** 2,699,969 Overture Maps Foundation building footprints; post-earthquake acquisitions cover 100% of the USGS ShakeMap MMI ≥ VI area.

## What's in this dataset

- `EMSR884_damage_confidence_20260701_v1.geojson` / `.gpkg` — confidence-tier quick-look layer: the 123,633 buildings flagged at any confidence tier, with `overture_id`, `damage_confidence` (possible 54,202 / probable 43,511 / high_confidence 25,920), and the binary `damage` flag (1 = probable or high_confidence; the 69,431 buildings with `damage` = 1).
- `EMSR884_analyzed_area_20260701_v1.geojson` / `.gpkg` — outline of where usable satellite coverage existed, so unassessed ground is not mistaken for undamaged.
- `EMSR884_adm2_damage_pct_20260701_v1.gpkg` — percent of assessed buildings damaged, by second-level administrative unit.

All layers are EPSG:4326 (WGS84) and open in QGIS, ArcGIS, geopandas, or R.

## README and Presentation

We have included a detailed README file and PowerPoint presentation in both English and Spanish below.

- `EMSR884_damage_20260701_v1_README.pdf` — detailed README: data description, methods, and agreement analyses (English).
- `EMSR884_damage_20260701_v1_README_ES.pdf` — the same README in Spanish.
- `EMSR884_damage_20260701_v1_slide_deck.pdf` — 32-slide briefing deck (English).
- `EMSR884_damage_20260701_v1_slide_deck_ES.pdf` — the same deck in Spanish.

Additionally, we have recorded a video presentation available in our mirrored directory.

## Citation

Cite as: Damage analysis of Copernicus Sentinel-1 data by Corey Scher and Jamon Van Den Hoek, Oregon State University. Overture Maps Foundation building footprints.

## Mirror

https://oregonstate.app.box.com/folder/394695539753?s=yrgtsbwmpqpajuhzioq0k13ihfluuneg

## NASA Disasters Portal Interactive Map

https://gis.earthdata.nasa.gov/portal/apps/mapviewer/index.html?webmap=0c3d77dd5aae46e4829d9a282477615c
